Christine’s mother’s mother was a Brooklyn girl of Irish blood.
Her father, Edward Duffy, born in New York in 1869, was very likely the son of Patrick and Catherine Duffy,
both born in Ireland. They were part of the great flight that began with the Famine of 1845 to 52,
when about a million people died and more than a million left, most of them for America.
The emigrants came through Castle Garden, New York’s landing depot from 1855, and many went no further than the harbour
cities: the men to the docks, the Navy Yard and the building trades, the women into service and the factories.
Frances Brady was a longshoreman’s daughter: in 1880 her father, very probably James Brady,
born in Ireland and brought over as a boy in the Famine years, worked the East River piers and lived on Furman Street,
under Brooklyn Heights; her mother was Catherine Creighton.
James died of tuberculosis on 3 May 1882, at about forty, in a six-family house on Garrison Street in the waterfront
Second Ward, and the next year’s city directory lists “Brady, Catharine, widow of James” at the same address,
left with three children under ten. Frances married Edward Duffy in April 1891,
by Maurice Wintrode’s family chart. In 1900 Edward, a driver, and Frances were living on North Elliott Place in Fort
Greene, near the Navy Yard, with Catherine, born in 1892, and three younger children.
On the evening of 9 October 1903 Edward very probably died suddenly of heart failure on North Portland Avenue,
around the corner, at about 34, leaving Frances, 28, with at least five children.
By 1905 she had remarried, and Catherine grew up as Catherine Winchell.
In 1910 she married Francis Jackson of Saint Louis.
They lived across the river in Hoboken, where Muriel was born in 1925, and Muriel grew up in Bay Ridge,
Brooklyn.
